claim: Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy (JME) is the most common form of idiopathic epilepsy in humans, making up 10–30% of cases.
source: Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy (JME) is the most common form of idiopathic epilepsy in humans, making up 10–30% of cases (Delgado-Escueta, 1984).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Delgado-Escueta, 1984.

claim: Disruption of EFHC1 has been reported as the most frequent cause of JME.
source: yet disruption of EFHC1, a non-ion channel protein, has been reported as the most frequent cause of JME (Delgado-Escueta, 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Delgado-Escueta, 2007.

claim: EFHC1 is specifically associated with motile cilia that project from specialized cells to enable fluid flow.
source: Interestingly, EFHC1 is also specifically associated with motile cilia that project from specialized cells to enable fluid flow (Conte et al., 2009; Suzuki et al., 2008; Suzuki et al., 2009)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Conte et al., 2009; Suzuki et al., 2008; Suzuki et al., 2009.

claim: In the human brain, there are both motile cilia, which enable cerebrospinal fluid flow, and non-motile cilia, which project from the cell bodies of all or most neurons.
source: In the human brain, there are both motile cilia, which enable cerebrospinal fluid flow, and non-motile cilia, which project from the cell bodies of all or most neurons (Bishop et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bishop et al., 2007.

claim: EFHC1 dysfunction impairs motility of ependymal cilia in mice.
source: Although EFHC1 dysfunction impairs motility of ependymal cilia in mice, the accompanying ventricle enlargement does not correlate with epilepsy (Suzuki et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Suzuki et al., 2009.

claim: The ventricle enlargement accompanying EFHC1 dysfunction in mice does not correlate with epilepsy.
source: Although EFHC1 dysfunction impairs motility of ependymal cilia in mice, the accompanying ventricle enlargement does not correlate with epilepsy (Suzuki et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Suzuki et al., 2009.

claim: EFHC1 is a core component of the protofilament ribbon structure of motile cilia thought to dictate the ordered attachment/arrangement of proteins required for motility.
source: As a core component of the protofilament ribbon structure of motile cilia thought to dictate the ordered attachment/arrangement of proteins required for motility (Ikeda et al., 2003; Linck et al., 2014)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ikeda et al., 2003; Linck et al., 2014.

claim: C. elegans EFHC-1 is required for mechanosensation in a class of non-motile cilia.
source: Here we demonstrate that rather than being a core component of ciliary motility-associated machinery, the C. elegans orthologue of EFHC-1 is required for mechanosensation in a class of non-motile cilia, where it regulates neuronal activation and dopamine signaling.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including calcium imaging and behavioral assays.

claim: C. elegans EFHC-1 regulates neuronal activation and dopamine signaling in non-motile cilia.
source: Here we demonstrate that rather than being a core component of ciliary motility-associated machinery, the C. elegans orthologue of EFHC-1 is required for mechanosensation in a class of non-motile cilia, where it regulates neuronal activation and dopamine signaling.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data including habituation assays and SWIP assays showing altered dopamine signaling in efhc-1 mutants.

claim: EFHC-1 localizes at the synapse where it modulates dopamine signaling in cooperation with the orthologue of an R-type voltage-gated calcium channel.
source: EFHC-1 also localizes at the synapse, where it further modulates dopamine signaling in cooperation with the orthologue of an R-type voltage-gated calcium channel.
evidence: The claim is supported by localization data showing EFHC-1 at synapses and genetic interaction data with unc-2.

claim: The efhc-1::gfp fusion construct is specifically expressed in dopaminergic CEP, ADE and PDE neurons, and glutamatergic OLQ neurons.
source: We generated a GFP reporter of C. elegans EFHC-1 driven by its own promoter, and found that the efhc-1::gfp fusion construct is specifically expressed in a small subset of ciliated mechanosensory neurons: the dopaminergic CEP, ADE and PDE neurons, and the glutamatergic OLQ neurons (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Four CEP neurons paired with four OLQ neurons project cilia in the nose.
source: four CEP neurons paired with four OLQ neurons project cilia in the nose, two ADE neurons position cilia in the anterior body, and two PDE neurons localize cilia to the posterior body (Inglis et al., 2007; Sulston et al., 1975; White et al., 1986) (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Inglis et al., 2007; Sulston et al., 1975; White et al., 1986 and Figure 1A.

claim: Two ADE neurons position cilia in the anterior body.
source: four CEP neurons paired with four OLQ neurons project cilia in the nose, two ADE neurons position cilia in the anterior body, and two PDE neurons localize cilia to the posterior body (Inglis et al., 2007; Sulston et al., 1975; White et al., 1986) (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Inglis et al., 2007; Sulston et al., 1975; White et al., 1986 and Figure 1A.

claim: Two PDE neurons localize cilia to the posterior body.
source: four CEP neurons paired with four OLQ neurons project cilia in the nose, two ADE neurons position cilia in the anterior body, and two PDE neurons localize cilia to the posterior body (Inglis et al., 2007; Sulston et al., 1975; White et al., 1986) (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Inglis et al., 2007; Sulston et al., 1975; White et al., 1986 and Figure 1A.

claim: EFHC-1::GFP is found in the distal regions of sex-specific dopaminergic ray neurons in the male tail.
source: Additionally, EFHC-1::GFP is found in the distal regions of sex-specific dopaminergic ray neurons in the male tail (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Endogenously GFP-tagged EFHC-1 predominantly accumulates in cilia of OLQ and ADE neurons.
source: Interestingly, while endogenously GFP-tagged EFHC-1 mostly accumulates in both OLQ and ADE cilia, it is weakly present in CEP cilia (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A)
evidence: The claim is supported by CRISPR knock-in data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Endogenously GFP-tagged EFHC-1 is weakly present in CEP cilia.
source: Interestingly, while endogenously GFP-tagged EFHC-1 mostly accumulates in both OLQ and ADE cilia, it is weakly present in CEP cilia (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A)
evidence: The claim is supported by CRISPR knock-in data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The C-terminal fragment of EFHC-1 containing the second DM10 domain specifically localizes to OLQ, CEP, ADE and PDE cilia.
source: Ciliary localization of EFHC-1 is further supported by the ability of a truncated protein (C-terminal fragment containing the second of two evolutionarily conserved DM10 domains of unknown function) to specifically localize to OLQ, CEP, ADE and PDE cilia in a manner indistinguishable from the full-length protein (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: The N-terminal fragment of EFHC-1 containing the first DM10 domain displays non-specific localization throughout all neuronal processes.
source: This is in contrast to a second truncated protein (N-terminal fragment containing the first DM10 domain) that displays non-specific localization throughout all neuronal processes of glutamatergic (OLQ) and dopaminergic (CEP, ADE and PDE) neurons (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: When distal or middle portions of CEP and OLQ cilia are photobleached, the EFHC-1::GFP signal does not rapidly recover within 30 s.
source: Consistent with this, when either the distal or middle portions of CEP and OLQ cilia are photobleached, the EFHC-1::GFP signal does not rapidly recover within 30 s, as would be expected for proteins dependent on diffusion to maintain their proper ciliary localizations, such as ARL-13 (Cevik et al., 2013) (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by FRAP data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4A–B.

claim: EFHC-1 proteins present in CEP and OLQ cilia are not associated with IFT.
source: Moreover, kymograph analyses suggest that EFHC-1 proteins present in CEP and OLQ cilia are not associated with IFT (Figure 1—figure supplement 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by kymograph analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4C.

claim: EFHC-1 localization is not dependent on UNC-101.
source: EFHC-1 localization is also not dependent on UNC-101, a protein required for dendritic transport and proper ciliary localization of a set of ciliary proteins (Dwyer et al., 2001) (Figure 1—figure supplement 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by localization data in unc-101 mutants shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4D.

claim: Ciliary expression of EFHC-1 is not dependent on DAF-19.
source: Interestingly, ciliary expression of EFHC-1 is not dependent on DAF-19 (Figure 1—figure supplement 4E), a transcription factor required for the expression of many ciliary genes
evidence: The claim is supported by expression data in daf-19 mutants shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4E.

claim: EFHC-1::GFP fusion protein is present at presynaptic regions in dopaminergic neurons, partially overlapping with the synaptic vesicle protein, synaptobrevin (SNB-1).
source: In addition to EFHC-1's ciliary localization, we find that the EFHC-1::GFP fusion protein is present at presynaptic regions in dopaminergic neurons, partially overlapping with the synaptic vesicle protein, synaptobrevin (SNB-1) (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by colocalization data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Endogenous EFHC-1 localizes to presynaptic regions where it partially overlaps with RAB-3.
source: By tagging endogenous EFHC-1 with GFP, we confirm that EFHC-1 localizes to these presynaptic regions, where it partially overlaps with a second synaptic vesicle protein (RAB-3) (Figure 1—figure supplement 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by CRISPR knock-in colocalization data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5A.

claim: EFHC-1 partially colocalizes with the active zone protein ELKS-1.
source: More specifically, EFHC-1 is found to partially colocalize with the active zone protein (ELKS-1) (Figure 1—figure supplement 5B–C)
evidence: The claim is supported by colocalization data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5B–C.

claim: UNC-104 is dispensable for EFHC-1 localization to presynaptic regions.
source: While RAB-3 localization is abrogated in unc-104 mutants, accumulating in cell bodies and diffusing to dendrites/axons of CEP neurons, UNC-104 is dispensable for both ELKS-1 and EFHC-1 localization (and consequently their partial colocalization pattern) to presynaptic regions (Figure 1—figure supplement 5A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by localization data in unc-104 mutants shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5A–C.

claim: Ciliary TRP-4 channels are mechanically activated in the presence of food, resulting in the release of dopamine.
source: In the presence of food, ciliary TRP-4 channels (orthologous to TRPN/NOMPC) are mechanically activated, resulting in the release of dopamine that modulates several behaviors through dopamine receptors (DOP-1, DOP-3 and DOP-4) on various postsynaptic/target cells (Chase et al., 2004; Ezcurra et al., 2011; Sanyal et al., 2004) (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Chase et al., 2004; Ezcurra et al., 2011; Sanyal et al., 2004 and Figure 2A.

claim: Disrupting tyrosine hydroxylase CAT-2 impairs dopamine signaling and prevents slowing in the presence of food.
source: Disrupting tyrosine hydroxylase, CAT-2, a rate-limiting enzyme for dopamine synthesis, impairs dopamine signaling and prevents slowing in the presence of food (Sawin et al., 2000) (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Sawin et al., 2000 and Figure 2A.

claim: Loss-of-function efhc-1(gk424336) mutants are able to slow in the presence of food.
source: In contrast, loss-of-function efhc-1(gk424336) mutants are able to slow in the presence of food (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: The claim is supported by basal slowing response data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: efhc-1 mutant males show mating potency similar to wild-type animals.
source: As expected, while cat-2 mutant males show reduced mating potency due to impaired dopamine signaling, efhc-1 mutant males show mating potency similar to wild-type animals (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by mating efficiency data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: efhc-1 mutants are able to release dopamine in appropriate behavioural contexts.
source: Together, these results show that efhc-1 mutants are able to release dopamine in appropriate behavioural contexts.
evidence: The claim is inferred from basal slowing and mating potency data.

claim: In the presence of food, efhc-1 mutants habituate slower than wild-type animals, and similar to dat-1 mutants.
source: In the presence of food, efhc-1 mutants habituate slower than wild-type animals, and similar to dat-1 mutants that have increased dopamine signaling (DA: dopamine). At each tap, the points represent the number of worms reversing over the total number of worms tracked per strain, and the error bars represent the binomial confidence intervals. Binomial logistic regression followed by Tukey's HSD (honest significant difference) test was used to determine significance of the habituated level (proportion reversing at tap 30) for each pair of strains. All strains are statistically different from each other (p < 0.001).
evidence: The claim is supported by tap habituation data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: A second allele of efhc-1, tm6235, leads to a slow habituation phenotype.
source: A second allele of efhc-1, tm6235, also leads to a slow habituation phenotype that is statistically different from wild-type (p < 0.001). All strains are statistically different from each other (p < 0.001).
evidence: The claim is supported by tap habituation data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The habituation phenotype seen in efhc-1 mutants is abolished in efhc-1;cat-2 double mutants.
source: The habituation phenotype seen in efhc-1 mutants is abolished in efhc-1;cat-2 double mutants, suggesting that the slow habituation phenotype of efhc-1 mutants depends on dopamine. All strains are statistically different from each other (p < 0.001) except for cat-2 and efhc-1;cat-2 (p = 0.69).
evidence: The claim is supported by tap habituation data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The slow habituation phenotype of efhc-1 mutants depends on dopamine.
source: The habituation phenotype seen in efhc-1 mutants is abolished in efhc-1;cat-2 double mutants, suggesting that the slow habituation phenotype of efhc-1 mutants depends on dopamine.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the genetic interaction data showing that cat-2 mutation suppresses the efhc-1 phenotype.

claim: efhc-1 mutants show defects in the dopamine-dependent swimming-induced paralysis phenotype, with an intermediate level of paralysis after 10 min compared to wild-type and dat-1 mutants.
source: efhc-1 mutants also show defects in the dopamine-dependent swimming-induced paralysis phenotype, with an intermediate level of paralysis after 10 min compared to wild-type and dat-1 mutants. Each bar represents the number of worms swimming after 10 min over the total number of worms per strain, and the error bars represent the binomial confidence intervals (n = 160 for each strain). Binomial logistic regression followed by Tukey's HSD (honest significant difference) test was used to determine significance for each pair of strains. All strains are statistically different from each other except for the two efhc-1 strains (ns = not significant, p = 0.115).
evidence: The claim is supported by SWIP data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: efhc-1 mutants show slower habituation compared to wild-type animals off food.
source: efhc-1 mutants show slower habituation compared to wild-type animals off food. At each tap, the points represent the number of worms reversing over the total number of worms tracked per strain, and the error bars represent the binomial confidence intervals. Binomial logistic regression followed by Tukey's HSD (honest significant difference) test was used to determine significance of the habituated level (proportion reversing at tap 30) for each pair of strains. All strains are statistically different from each other (p < 0.001).
evidence: The claim is supported by tap habituation data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: efhc-1 mutants off food mimic the habituation seen in wild-type animals on food.
source: efhc-1 mutants off food mimic the habituation phenotype of wild-type animals on food, while dat-1 mutants habituate slightly slower than efhc-1 mutants off food Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by tap habituation data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Both efhc-1 alleles show intermediate thrashing frequencies compared to wild-type and dat-1 mutants.
source: Whereas most wild-type animals continue swimming 10 min after being submersed in water, most dat-1 animals are paralysed (Figure 2E), exhibiting an average thrashing frequency consistently lower than wild-type animals (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D). In this assay, both efhc-1 alleles show intermediate levels of paralysis at 10 min compared to wild-type and dat-1 mutants (Figure 2E), and corresponding intermediate thrashing frequencies (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by thrashing frequency data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2D.

claim: efhc-1 mutants have increased dopamine signaling compared to wild-type animals, but less than dat-1 mutants.
source: Together, our data are consistent with efhc-1 mutants having increased dopamine signaling compared to wild-type animals, but less than dat-1 mutants.
evidence: The claim is inferred from multiple behavioral assays including habituation and SWIP.

claim: Wild-type animals show a calcium response to gentle (buzz) and strong (press) mechanical stimuli to the nose ~50% of the time.
source: Wild-type animals show a calcium response to each stimulus ~50% of the time, as measured by a change in the YFP/CFP ratio (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: efhc-1(gk424336) mutants rarely respond upon gentle stimulation but respond at wild-type levels to stronger stimulation.
source: In contrast, efhc-1(gk424336) mutants rarely respond upon gentle stimulation but respond at wild-type levels to the stronger stimulation (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: When efhc-1 mutants do exhibit calcium responses to either stimulus, they are of a comparable amplitude and shape as wild-type responses.
source: Interestingly, when efhc-1 mutants do exhibit calcium responses to either stimulus, they are of a comparable amplitude and shape as wild-type responses (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: EFHC-1 has a specific role in mediating the likelihood of mechanosensory transduction upon gentle stimulation.
source: This suggests that like TRP-4, EFHC-1 has a specific role in mediating the likelihood of mechanosensory transduction upon gentle stimulation, as seen when an animal encounters food.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the similarity of efhc-1 and trp-4 phenotypes in calcium imaging experiments.

claim: Mechanosensory transduction in non-dopaminergic OLQ neurons is not impaired in efhc-1 mutants.
source: In contrast, mechanosensory transduction in non-dopaminergic OLQ neurons is not impaired in efhc-1 mutants and OLQ-mediated foraging behaviors are similarly unaffected (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging and behavioral data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–E.

claim: EFHC-1 has a specific mechanosensory function in CEP dopaminergic neurons.
source: This implies a specific mechanosensory function for EFHC-1 in CEP dopaminergic neurons.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that EFHC-1 affects mechanosensation in CEP but not OLQ neurons.

claim: The axonemal structure of CEP neurons is not abrogated in efhc-1 mutants.
source: The axonemal structure of CEP neurons by TEM cross-section (refer to schematic) is not abrogated in efhc-1 mutants. Scale bars, 100 nm.
evidence: The claim is supported by TEM data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The localization of TRP-4 is unaffected in efhc-1 mutants.
source: The localization of the mechanosensory channel, TRP-4, which is comparable to that of EFHC-1, is unaffected in efhc-1 mutants.
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Lengths of CEP and OLQ cilia measured in trp-4 and trp-4;efhc-1 mutants are indistinguishable.
source: Lengths of CEP and OLQ cilia measured in trp-4 and trp-4;efhc-1 mutants are indistinguishable. Each dot represents one cilium. Kruskal-Wallis rank sum test (CEP cilia lengths) and Tukey's Honest Significant Differences (OLQ cilia lengths) were used for calculating the statistical significance. ns, not significant.
evidence: The claim is supported by ciliary length measurements shown in Figure 3D.

claim: EFHC-1 does not play an essential role in specifying or maintaining non-motile cilia ultrastructure.
source: Hence, EFHC-1 does not play an essential role in specifying, or maintaining, non-motile cilia ultrastructure in this metazoan.
evidence: The claim is inferred from TEM data showing normal ciliary structure in efhc-1 mutants.

claim: Synaptic regions are intact in efhc-1 mutants.
source: We first confirmed that synaptic regions are intact in efhc-1 mutants (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: efhc-1;trp-4 double mutants show slower habituation than trp-4 mutants.
source: Interestingly, efhc-1;trp-4 double mutants show slower habituation than trp-4 mutants (Figure 4A), consistent with a rise in dopamine signaling independent of ciliary TRP-4-associated mechanosensation.
evidence: The claim is supported by tap habituation data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Loss of EFHC-1 function at the synapse may inappropriately stimulate dopamine release in the absence of TRP-4-mediated mechanosensation.
source: In other words, loss of EFHC-1 function at the synapse may inappropriately stimulate dopamine release in the absence of TRP-4-mediated mechanosensation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the genetic interaction between efhc-1 and trp-4.

claim: efhc-1;daf-19 double mutants show responsiveness and habituation phenotypes that are intermediate between the daf-19 and efhc-1 single mutants.
source: In contrast, the efhc-1;daf-19 double mutants show responsiveness and habituation phenotypes that are intermediate between the daf-19 and efhc-1 single mutants (Figure 4B)
evidence: The claim is supported by tap habituation data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The loss of EFHC-1 results in increased dopamine signaling downstream of ciliary function.
source: In contrast, the efhc-1;daf-19 double mutants show responsiveness and habituation phenotypes that are intermediate between the daf-19 and efhc-1 single mutants (Figure 4B), again suggesting that the loss of EFHC-1 results in increased dopamine signaling downstream of ciliary function.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the genetic interaction between efhc-1 and daf-19.

claim: EFHC1 physically interacts with and modulates the alpha subunit of the R-type voltage-gated calcium channel in humans.
source: In humans, EFHC1 physically interacts with and modulates the alpha subunit of the R-type voltage-gated calcium channel (Suzuki et al., 2004), which is most closely related to UNC-2 in C. elegans.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Suzuki et al., 2004.

claim: The R-type voltage-gated calcium channel in humans is most closely related to UNC-2 in C. elegans.
source: In humans, EFHC1 physically interacts with and modulates the alpha subunit of the R-type voltage-gated calcium channel (Suzuki et al., 2004), which is most closely related to UNC-2 in C. elegans.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge of orthology relationships.

claim: unc-2 gain-of-function mutants show slow habituation compared to both wild-type animals and efhc-1 mutants.
source: Since unc-2 mutants are uncoordinated and cannot be tested for habituation defects, we took advantage of a gain-of-function (gf) allele that shows slow habituation compared to both wild-type animals and efhc-1 mutants (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by tap habituation data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Expressing overactive UNC-2 specifically in efhc-1-expressing cells results in a slow habituation phenotype similar to that seen in efhc-1 mutants.
source: Remarkably, expressing overactive UNC-2 specifically in efhc-1-expressing cells results in a slow habituation phenotype similar (but not identical) to that seen in efhc-1 mutants; crossing the UNC-2(gf) construct into efhc-1 mutants did not result in slower habituation, but instead leads to habituation similar to that seen in animals with UNC-2(gf) specifically in efhc-1-expressing cells (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by tap habituation data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: EFHC-1 may negatively regulate UNC-2, such that loss of EFHC-1 results in maximum activation of the voltage-gated channel at the synapse.
source: Our findings therefore provide evidence that independent of its sensory/activation role at the cilium, EFHC-1 may negatively regulate UNC-2, such that loss of EFHC-1 results in maximum activation of the voltage-gated channel at the synapse.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the genetic interaction data between efhc-1 and unc-2(gf).

claim: EFHC1 has been adapted to function in a specific class of non-motile ciliated mechanosensory cells in C. elegans.
source: Our work in a representative eumetazoan (C. elegans) that lacks motile cilia supports this idea, where EFHC-1 has been adapted to function in a specific class of non-motile ciliated mechanosensory cells, the dopaminergic neurons (see model in Figure 5), where it is required for mechanosensation and proper dopamine signaling, yet dispensable for non-motile ciliary structure.
evidence: The claim is supported by the collective experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: EFHC1 may have adapted its mechanosensation role from motile cilia to a strictly sensory role in non-motile cilia.
source: Our findings suggest that EFHC1, by being an integral part of the ciliary axoneme and by potentially modulating TRP (or other types of) mechanosensitive calcium channels (Katano et al., 2012) may have adapted its mechanosensation role from motile cilia (e.g., for environmental sensing and/or internal sensation and regulation of motile cilium movement) to a strictly sensory role in non-motile cilia.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from the data and a citation to Katano et al., 2012.

claim: EFHC-1 functions at the synapses of dopaminergic neurons in C. elegans.
source: We also find that in C. elegans, EFHC-1 functions at the synapses of dopaminergic neurons (Figure 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by localization and functional data presented in the manuscript.

claim: UNC-2 localizes to presynaptic active zones of sensory neurons.
source: Importantly, this role is also likely related to the modulation of a calcium channel, namely UNC-2, that localizes to presynaptic active zones of sensory neurons (Saheki and Bargmann, 2009)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Saheki and Bargmann, 2009.

claim: UNC-2 may play an important role in evoked neurotransmitter release.
source: Importantly, this role is also likely related to the modulation of a calcium channel, namely UNC-2, that localizes to presynaptic active zones of sensory neurons (Saheki and Bargmann, 2009), where it may play an important role in evoked neurotransmitter release (Mathews et al., 2003; Richmond et al., 2001; Schafer and Kenyon, 1995).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Mathews et al., 2003; Richmond et al., 2001; Schafer and Kenyon, 1995.

claim: Inappropriate regulation of dopamine signaling may contribute to various forms of epilepsy.
source: By identifying an epilepsy-related protein that directly modulates dopamine signaling in C. elegans, our work helps to strengthen the potential link between dopamine signaling and epilepsy, where evidence is accumulating to suggest that inappropriate regulation of dopamine signaling may contribute to various forms of epilepsy (Bozzi and Borrelli, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bozzi and Borrelli, 2013.

claim: JME patients display several deficits in cognitive functions influenced by dopamine.
source: A role for dopamine is particularly relevant in JME because patients also display several deficits in cognitive functions influenced by dopamine, such as behavioral disturbances, social integration problems, impaired executive functions, reduced cognitive speed and impaired working memory (Bailet and Turk, 2000; Devinsky et al., 1997; Janz, 1985; Pascalicchio et al., 2007; Swartz et al., 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bailet and Turk, 2000; Devinsky et al., 1997; Janz, 1985; Pascalicchio et al., 2007; Swartz et al., 1996.

claim: Dopamine signaling is dysregulated in JME patients.
source: Interrogation of the dopaminergic system in JME patients has revealed that dopamine signaling is indeed dysregulated in JME patients (Ciumas et al., 2008; Ciumas et al., 2010; Odano et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ciumas et al., 2008; Ciumas et al., 2010; Odano et al., 2012.

claim: Dopamine may play a role in the onset of seizures and/or cognitive impairments associated with JME.
source: In combination with our work, this suggests that dopamine may play a role in the onset of seizures and/or cognitive impairments associated with JME.
evidence: The claim is speculative, inferred from the combination of the authors' data and literature on dopamine dysregulation in JME.

claim: Dopamine receptors (DRD1, 2, 5) are found on cilia.
source: Indeed, dopamine receptors (DRD1, 2, 5) themselves are found on cilia, as are numerous other receptors, including for serotonin, Melanin-concentrating hormone, somatostatin, galanin, and neuropeptide (FF/YY) (Hilgendorf et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hilgendorf et al., 2016.

claim: Cilia may modulate neuronal excitation thresholds and play important roles in collectively influencing behavior, energy homeostasis and other aspects of mammalian physiology.
source: In such neurons (and others), cilia may modulate neuronal excitation thresholds and thus play important roles in collectively influencing behavior, energy homeostasis and other aspects of mammalian physiology.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from the authors' findings in C. elegans and knowledge of ciliary receptors.
